problem: Existing VLN agents attend softly over individual instruction words and ignore syntactic structure (phrases, modifiers, word function), so cross-modal alignment is shallow and generalizes poorly to unseen environments.
motivation: Dependency parse trees group syntactically related words into phrases that correspond to sub-instructions/actions and expose modifiers such as direction words. Injecting this structure should give phrase-level grounding and reduce word-level overfitting.
key_idea: Encode the instruction with a Bi-LSTM followed by a ChildSum Tree-LSTM over its dependency tree, and attend over the resulting syntax-aware node representations at each navigation step.
insight: Explicit syntax gives gains beyond added parameters: on R2R val-unseen the syntax agent gets 49.0 SR vs 46.4 for a 2-layer LSTM baseline with a comparable parameter increase. Replacing the Tree-LSTM with mean pooling costs about 3% SR, and a constituency tree costs about 2% SR, so the tree recurrence and dependency structure both matter. Gains on RxR vary by language (Hindi +2.6 SR, English +0.7, Telugu +0.1), which the authors attribute to parser quality.
method: Dependency parsing: Stanford CoreNLP for English, Stanza for Hindi and Telugu, gives a dependency tree per instruction.
Syntax-aware encoder: embedding, then Bi-LSTM to preserve word order, then ChildSum Tree-LSTM over the dependency tree; every node yields a representation u_dep_i.
Language grounding: at each step, soft attention over all tree-node representations, conditioned on the decoder state h_t, gives u~_t; h~_t = tanh(W_M[u~_t; h_t]).
Visual encoder and decoder: ResNet-152 features for 36 panoramic views plus orientation; attention over views, LSTM decoder, and softmax over navigable viewpoints (EnvDrop architecture).
Training: mixed imitation learning (teacher forcing on the shortest path) and A2C reinforcement learning (+1/-1 progress reward, +3/-3 stop reward), lambda=0.2, without back-translation augmentation.
Variants: mean pooling instead of Tree-LSTM and a constituency-tree Tree-LSTM, both worse. The +LSTM control uses a 2-layer LSTM for comparable capacity.

setting.backbone: EnvDrop-style LSTM seq2seq agent + Bi-LSTM/Tree-LSTM encoder + ResNet-152 features (trained from scratch, without back-translation)
setting.training_data: R2R train (14,025 instructions, 61 envs); RxR guide paths only (11,089 paths, 3 languages); no augmentation data
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views, ResNet-152 features) with heading/elevation
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (navigable locations, or STOP)
setting.privileged: none (dependency parses are computed from instruction text by off-the-shelf parsers)

numbers.evidence: Table 2, comparison with and without tree-based encoder, Val Unseen

numbers.extra: no back-translation augmentation; R2R test leaderboard
numbers.evidence: Our syntax-aware agent achieves 47.8% in success rate and 0.45 in SPL

numbers_note: RxR test-leaderboard results (SAA mono) are given only as relative gains (nDTW +5.73%, SR +9.98% over the RxR baseline), not absolute values, so they are not listed. SPL, nDTW, SDTW and CLS are printed as fractions (0-1) in the paper, while SR is in percent.
results: The syntax-aware agent improves the EnvDrop baseline on R2R val-unseen from 45.3 to 49.0 SR (+3.7) and beats the +LSTM control (46.4). On the R2R test leaderboard it reaches 47.8 SR / 0.45 SPL, +2.1 SR over the baseline. On RxR it improves all three languages on val-unseen (largest gain Hindi, 39.9 to 42.5 SR) and was state of the art on RxR at submission.
limitations: Depends on dependency parser quality; gains are small for Telugu and English, where parser quality may limit the benefit
Large seen/unseen gap remains, and the model is evaluated only in simulation
Compared mainly against a re-implemented EnvDrop without back-translation, so gains over stronger pretrained VLN models are untested
